description: Language-agnostic EIP-681 conformance vectors. Expectations are authored from the EIP-681 specification text and from defects observed in real parsers; they are NOT generated from any single implementation's output. A conforming parser must reproduce `expect` for every case. Fields under `expect.fields` are checked only when ok is true.

fields_checked.ok: boolean — no errors present (warnings may exist)
fields_checked.error_codes: array of strings — each MUST appear in the parser's error list when ok=false
fields_checked.warning_codes: array of strings — each MUST appear in the warning list
fields_checked.fields: semantic values that must match when ok=true: chainId (integer|null), amount (decimal string|null), recipient (lowercase hex or null), target (lowercase hex or null), isTokenTransfer (boolean)

notes: C-* = address handling. S-* = structural. A-* = amount. T-* = token transfer. X-* = cross-cutting hazards.

vectors.why: Baseline: the minimal well-formed native transfer.
No scheme separator before the address: not a URI with a scheme at all.
EIP-681 fixes the scheme as 'ethereum'. A different one names a different payment system.
Empty string is not a URI.
Scheme present but no target address.
Scheme comparison is case-insensitive per RFC 3986; 'Ethereum:' names the same scheme.
The 'pay-' prefix is deprecated but must still parse; ignoring it would make the parser reject a legal URI.
Uppercase hex in the target body with no mixed case is not a checksum claim.
A 20-byte address is exactly 40 hex digits. This is the accepted baseline for every length case below.
39 digits = 19.5 bytes. Not an address.

REAL DEFECT CLASS: grammars written as a minimum (parse_min(40)) inherit no ceiling, so 41 digits reach the checksum step. Observed upstream: an over-length native recipient was returned as a valid ERC-55 address instead of rejected.
42 digits — the single sample most length bugs are tested against; a 41..64 sweep catches what a lone 42 does not.
48 digits — a common truncation/padding boundary in fixed-width encoders.
64 digits — exactly 32 bytes, so it fits a bytes32 slot and can survive a naive hex-to-bytes conversion.
Mixed case IS an EIP-55 checksum claim. This is canonical vector #2 written with WRONG casing so the claim fails; accepting it means paying an address the string does not describe.
Canonical EIP-55 vector #2, correct casing. Must be accepted.
Canonical EIP-55 vector #1.
Canonical EIP-55 vector #3.
All-lowercase makes no checksum claim and must not be rejected — a parser that demands mixed case breaks most real QRs.
The zero address is syntactically valid and unrecoverable. Emitting it is always a bug; refusing is safer than warning.
EIP-681 spec example: scientific notation with a decimal mantissa, exact value required.
Plain decimal integer.
Base units are indivisible, so a fractional amount cannot be expressed. Silently truncating would pay a different number than written.
Negative amounts are meaningless in this scheme.
uint256 maximum must survive without precision loss — the classic JSON float hazard.
A bare exponent with no mantissa is not a number.
Empty value parameter.
EIP-155 chain ids start at 1. '@0' names a network that does not exist, so the destination is undefined.
Chain id is present but empty.
A chain id beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER cannot be represented exactly; accepting it risks silently changing the network.
Missing chain id is legal per the grammar but hazardous: the same contract address exists on many chains. Must parse, and must be flagged.
Hex chain id is a common extension and must be read as a number, not a string.
Canonical ERC-20 transfer. Target is the TOKEN CONTRACT; `address` is the human recipient.
HIGH-SEVERITY HAZARD: omitting uint256 is grammar-valid, but some parsers read it as a fixed zero transfer and others as an open-ended amount the user authorises. Must parse and must be flagged.
No recipient means the tokens have no destination that a wallet can show the user.
REAL DEFECT CLASS: a deposit QR that puts the ERC-20 CONTRACT in `address` makes any parser read the contract as the payee. A parser must not conflate target with recipient.
vectors.note: Legal but semantically identical target and recipient: the caller must be able to SEE that they are equal and decide. A parser that hides `target` makes this indistinguishable from T-01.

vectors.why: `value` alongside `uint256` is ambiguous: to one parser the number is token base units, to another it is native currency. Two fields, one transfer, one of them silently ignored.
vectors.note: `amount` MUST be null here. When ok=false the ambiguous figure must not be exposed, or a caller testing `amount !== null` pays a silently chosen number.

vectors.why: uint256 is only defined by EIP-681 inside /transfer. At the top level of a native request, and inside any other function, its meaning depends on an ABI the URI does not carry — so it must not be silently accepted as an amount.
An over-length address in `address=` (the recipient slot) is as dangerous as one in the target: 41 hex digits.
An over-length TOKEN CONTRACT address is the third call site of the same length check and the one most test suites omit.
Recipient is the zero address — tokens are burned.
A token transfer of exactly zero is legal but almost always a mistake; flag, do not reject.
A mixed-case recipient with a failing checksum claim. Warning rather than error is the defensible choice here (the field is a parameter, not the target), but it must not pass silently.
CROSS-CUTTING: the same address on two chains is two different accounts. A URI without a chain id that is fed to a wallet defaulting to the wrong network pays the wrong place.
Query parameters are separated by '&'. A parser that splits on the first '?' only, or that fails to stop at a fragment, mis-reads the amount.
Leading and trailing whitespace is common when a URI is extracted from a QR or a line of text; trimming is safe and must not change semantics.

An APPROVAL is not a payment. EIP-681 defines uint256 only for /transfer, so inside /approve the number depends on an ABI the URI does not carry: refusing it is the safe behaviour. What must NOT happen is an approval being reported as a transfer.

The same approval-shaped URI WITHOUT uint256 must still parse, and must report isTokenTransfer=false. If every function collapsed to isTokenTransfer=true, an unlimited token approval would be shown to the user as an ordinary payment.
A 41-digit token address plus a 41-digit recipient: two independent length failures. Reporting only the first hides the second.
